acquisition.why: This kind of community grows almost entirely from the founder's audience and personal brand (Mike's YouTube and podcast). Ricardo has no audience and no agency track record, so agents posting content would struggle to build trust [E]. The channels themselves (inbound content and ads) are legal.

onboarding.why: Joining through Skool/Circle plus Stripe is self-serve.

delivery.why: Members pay for live calls, feedback and credibility from someone who has done it. AI can draft lessons, but people won't value coaching from an unproven operator.

support.why: Engaging with the community and answering member questions needs a credible human every week.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has no audience or agency results, and 6-8 h/week can't support the community engagement and credibility this needs. Claims come from a founder promoting his own community. Selling courses about income opportunities also carries UK ASA/CMA risk around earnings claims.
scores.M_why: The 'start an AI agency' coaching market is saturated with personality-led communities and free YouTube content. Differentiation comes from the founder's reputation, which Ricardo doesn't have.
scores.one_line: Five videos, but all one founder self-promoting member counts on one channel. The model depends on personal reputation and live engagement, a poor fit for an agent-run part-timer with no audience.

acquisition.why: Inbound channels (app stores, SEO, paid ads) are all legal. However, discovery is crowded and app-store/ad-dependent, and paid UA economics are tough at $10/month.

delivery.why: LLM API behind a user interface, unattended.

support.why: Agents can handle FAQs and refunds. Hallucination complaints and edge cases need occasional human review.

scores.R_why: Ricardo is technical, so building an MVP for under £300 is easy. He would need to handle UK GDPR, provider terms, and profession-specific liability (legal, medical, financial). The hard part is distribution, not the build.
scores.M_why: By 2026, thin wrappers are being commoditised directly by ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini features and by many copycats. Only deep vertical workflow and data moats survive [E].
scores.one_line: Highly automatable and cheap to test, but generic wrappers are heavily commoditised. There is no first-hand evidence, and the claims are mostly hypothetical. Viable only with a narrow UK vertical workflow and an SEO/marketplace channel.

acquisition.why: Etsy, Amazon UK and eBay marketplaces plus Meta ads are all inbound and legal. This is highly platform-dependent.

onboarding.why: Marketplace checkout. Custom busts need scan intake and back-and-forth.

delivery.why: Physical printing, post-processing, packing and posting need hands every day. Print-farm outsourcing (e.g. UK print services) is possible, but margins shrink [E].

support.why: Agents can handle messages. Damages, returns and refunds need occasional human decisions.

scores.R_why: A test fits the £300 budget (one Bambu-class printer at ~£300-500 [E]). But a print farm needs space, hours and physical labour that a toddler parent with 6-8 h/week lacks. UK GPSR product-safety rules and IP/licensing risk on gaming accessories also apply.
scores.M_why: Niche accessories still have headroom, but they're hit-driven with short product lives. Expect copycats, leaked STLs and injection-moulded undercutting. Etsy UK 3D-print categories are crowded.
scores.one_line: Well-evidenced first-hand numbers from one operator. But this is physical, labour-heavy fulfilment that agents can't run. Good business, wrong fit unless production is outsourced.

acquisition.why: Inbound channels work: SEO, submissions from tool makers, and developer communities. Agents can produce programmatic SEO pages, though this depends on Google.

onboarding.why: Self-serve listing submission and paid sponsorship checkout. Agents can moderate.

delivery.why: Agents can scrape and refresh listings from GitHub and registries. Human spot checks for quality.

billing.why: Stripe works for featured listings. Selling sponsorship packages may need occasional negotiation.

support.why: Low-touch: listing edits and removal requests.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it cheaply and it fits his technical skill and limited hours. Monetisation is slow: it needs traffic before sponsors pay, and revenue claims are unproven [E].
scores.M_why: AI/dev tool directories are massively saturated (Product Hunt, DevHunt, thousands of AI directories). Official MCP registries are commoditising MCP lists, and AI search erodes directory SEO.
scores.one_line: Very agent-friendly and cheap to run, but the evidence is only interest signals, not revenue. The niche is crowded and threatened by official registries and AI search, so it only works in a sharply defined underserved niche.

acquisition.why: SEO and content are possible, but the source relied on a podcast audience. UK financial-promotion rules constrain ad copy and backtest claims, and Google/Meta require financial-services verification for some ads.

delivery.why: Automated scoring, alerts and backtests. Data licensing needs care: Yahoo Finance terms forbid commercial use, so a paid data feed is required [E].

scores.R_why: Technically easy for Ricardo. However, the FCA perimeter (whether it counts as personal recommendations), financial-promotion rules, and the cost of a licensed market-data feed eat a £300 budget. Showing past performance like '29% vs 8.4%' invites regulatory trouble.
scores.M_why: Crowded field (Finviz, Koyfin, Stock Rover, AI screeners in brokers), and $5-10/month retail churn is high. The thesis angle is a gimmick that is easily copied.
scores.one_line: Highly automatable, but the claims rest on a survivorship-biased backtest. UK FCA/promotion risk and data-licensing costs make it a poor fit despite simple delivery.

acquisition.why: Organic X/Instagram content and UGC can be largely agent-produced, but personal-brand building is founder-driven. The cold DM tactic used in the source breaches PECR in the UK and must be dropped.

onboarding.why: Paste a link and get clips; self-serve.

delivery.why: Unattended cloud processing via Gemini API.

support.why: Credit disputes, abuse and rendering failures need routine human checks.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it, but competing requires constant iteration and a personal brand. The source founder spends roughly $400-600/month on agent tooling, and rendering and API costs exceed a £300 test. Copyright liability from users clipping third-party content also applies.
scores.M_why: A red-ocean market: Opus Clip ($50M raised), Vizard, Descript, CapCut and native YouTube/TikTok clipping tools. Churn is 1-3 months and margins are thin.
scores.one_line: Solid first-hand MRR evidence and fully automatable delivery. But the market is crowded by funded players and platform-native features, and acquisition relied on founder brand plus PECR-unsafe DMs.

acquisition.why: Content, SEO and YouTube inbound are legal, but the source relied on the founder's creator audience.

delivery.why: Gemini video analysis and generation run unattended. Output quality varies.

scores.R_why: Cheap to build with Gemini, which suits Ricardo's skills and time. There is no pricing or revenue evidence, and he has no creator audience to seed it.
scores.M_why: vidIQ, TubeBuddy, 1of10, YouTube's own AI inspiration tools, and anyone with Gemini can replicate it. The commoditisation risk is extreme.
scores.one_line: Easy to automate but thinly evidenced (no revenue or pricing) and trivially copyable over Gemini. The market is crowded, including platform-native YouTube features.

acquisition.why: Organic social growth is the product itself, inbound and legal. Agents can schedule posts, but the channel depends entirely on algorithms and account-ban risk.

onboarding.why: No customer onboarding; followers just follow.

delivery.why: AI generation and scheduling pipelines (Veo, Bannerbear, Hopper) can run mostly unattended. Content selection and quality need human taste.

billing.why: Monetisation is indirect: creator payouts (limited UK eligibility), brand deals needing negotiation, or affiliate links. Nothing direct to bill.

support.why: Little customer support, but comment and DM moderation and handling platform strikes are needed.

scores.R_why: Cheap and low-hours to start, but UK fair dealing doesn't cover reposting others' videos, so only original or AI-generated content is safe. Monetisation is unproven in the dossier, and brand-deal income needs human selling. Platforms are increasingly demoting AI slop and reused content.
scores.M_why: Faceless and AI-character pages are saturated in 2026, and platforms penalise unoriginal and AI-generated content. It is pure platform risk, though niche UK audiences remain open.
scores.one_line: Eight videos, but only reach claims with no evidence of income. Repost models carry copyright risk in the UK, and AI-content monetisation is indirect and platform-fragile. Better as a distribution asset than a standalone business.
